newsitem.title: USA: Producer prices fell in April.
newsitem.headline: Producer prices fell in April.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent
Producer prices tumbled in April, posting their biggest drop in nearly four years, the government said Wednesday in a report that tempered but did not extinguish worries about higher interest rates.

Prices at the wholesale level fell 0.6 percent last month, the fourth straight monthly decline, as prices on everything from vegetables to computers declined, the Labour Department said. Prices fell 0.1 percent in March.

Stock and bond prices rallied after the report, which some analysts said reduced the odds that the Federal Reserve would raise rates again when its policy-makers meet on Tuesday, though stocks later gave back much of the gains.
"The Fed appears on an economic and political hotspot," said Alan Ackerman, senior vice president at Fahnestock and Co. "Inflation numbers remain relatively benign."

The Dow Jones industrial average jumped 75 points in early trading but later backed off to end 11.95 points higher at 7,286.16. The 30-year Treasury rose a half point, or $5 on a $1,000 bond, and its yield fell to 6.88 percent from 6.93 percent on Tuesday. The bond's price and yield move in opposite directions.
Wall Street analysts, who had expected producer prices to hold steady in April, were surprised by last month's decline, which was the biggest since August 1993.

"It's certainly better than what investors had anticipated," said Kevin Flanagan, vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc. "It will have to enter into discussions at the Fed."
But other analysts said the drop was unlikely on its own to prevent a rate rise by the central bank, which is concerned that the economy is growing too quickly for its own good.

Fed policy-makers have been more concerned with upward pressure on wages after more than six years of economic growth. The Fed raised short-term rates a quarter point on March 25, the first increase in more than two years, and Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan said the central bank's move was meant to ward off inflation before it becomes a big problem.
"We don't want irrational exuberance in the whole economy," said former Fed Chairman Paul Volcker, alluding to his successor's comment last year about a frothy stock market.
"Some of the preconditions (for inflation) are there," he said in an interview with CNBC television, pointing in particular to the tight job markets.
Last month's decline in producer prices was led by another drop in energy costs, which fell 2.6 percent.

After surging in March, food prices fell in April. Prices for vegetables tumbled 20 percent and fruit prices fell about 5 percent. The recent steep rise in coffee prices slowed, with prices up 5 percent after a 13 percent March rise.
Excluding food and energy costs, which can vary widely month to month, producer prices fell 0.1 percent in April, after a 0.4 percent rise in March.

Prices for a variety of other goods also declined. Auto prices fell 0.5 percent, computer prices dropped 4.1 percent and aircraft prices declined 2 percent. Tobacco prices, which rose 2.5 percent in March, increased 0.9 percent in April.
The report also showed little inflationary pressure in the production pipeline.
Prices of intermediate goods, items used to make finished products, fell 0.3 percent in April. Prices of crude goods used at the start of production dropped 0.9 percent.

"Right now it doesn't look like there's a lot of inflation potential," said Norbert Ore, who heads the widely watched monthly surveys by the National Association of Purchasing Management, whose members buy materials for about 300 major corporations.
The steep drop in producer prices last month overshadowed a separate report from the Commerce Department that business inventories rose again in March.

Business inventories grew 0.3 percent to a seasonally adjusted $1.02 billion, after a revised 0.4 percent jump in February. The data, the latest pointing to a tapering off in demand, followed news on Tuesday that retail sales fell 0.3 percent in April, the biggest drop in 10 months.
